'''Samuel Emmett Horne Jr.''' (July 26, 1924 –February 4, 2006)<ref>{{cite book|title=[[International Rubber Science Hall of Fame]]|date=2010|publisher=University of Akron}}</ref> was a research scientist at [[B. F. Goodrich]] noted for first synthesizing cis-1,4-[[polyisoprene]],<ref>{{cite journal|last=Horne Jr.|first=S. E.|title=Polymerization of Diene Monomers by Ziegler Type Catalysis|journal=Rubber Chemistry and Technology|date=1980|volume=53|issue=3|pages=71–79|doi=10.5254/1.3535055}}</ref> the main polymer contained in natural tree rubber, using [[Ziegler–Natta catalyst|Ziegler catalysis]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Hoff|first=Ray, Robert T. Mathers|title=Handbook of Transition Metal Polymerization Catalysts|date=2010|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=9780470504420|page=539}}</ref> [[Charles Greville Williams|Earlier attempts to produce synthetic rubber from isoprene]] had been unsuccessful, but in 1955, Horne prepared 98 percent cis-1,4-polyisoprene via the [[Stereoisomerism|stereospecific polymerization]] of [[isoprene]]. The product of this reaction differs from [[natural rubber]] only slightly.  It contains a small amount of cis-1,2-polyisoprene, but it is indistinguishable from natural rubber in its physical properties.<ref>{{cite book |title=Worldwide Rubber Statistics. |date=2008 |publisher=International Institute of Synthetic Rubber Producers, Inc (IISRP)}}</ref>

==Personal==
Horne was born July 26, 1924, in [[Jacksonville, Florida]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Fawcett|first=Robert J.|title=Sam Horne Biography at IRSHF induction|date=2010|publisher=University of Akron|location=Akron, Ohio}}</ref> He grew up in [[Tampa, Florida]]. He married Sue Ross in 1949. They had four children.

He showed interest in chemistry at a young age.  When he was five or six years old, he and a friend played with a chemistry set. Although the experiments sometimes led to unpleasant odors and other problems, his parents nevertheless encouraged the young Horne to pursue his interest in chemistry.

Horne died on February 4, 2006, in [[Columbus, Ohio]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Noga|first=Ed|title=A Man of Science|accessdate=26 March 2014|newspaper=Rubber & Plastics News|date=March 2006|volume= 35 |issue= 16|page=8|url=http://connection.ebscohost.com/c/editorials/20038809/man-science|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303220254/http://connection.ebscohost.com/c/editorials/20038809/man-science|url-status=dead|archive-date=2016-03-03}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Horne graduated from Tampa's [[Henry B. Plant High School]] in 1942. He enrolled at [[Emory University]], but his university studies were interrupted by [[World War II]]. He joined the U.S. Navy in July 1943 and served until 1946. He was released to inactive status with the rank of [[Lieutenant (JG)]].

He returned to Emory University, where he obtained his A.B. degree in 1947, his M.A. degree in 1948, and his Ph.D. degree in 1950. After graduating, Horne took a job at the [[B. F. Goodrich]] Company's Research and Development Center in [[Brecksville, Ohio]] in 1950. He remained with B.F Goodrich until it sold its rubber research division to the Canadian company Polysar in 1982. He retired from Polysar in 1987.<ref name=":0" />

==Research==
{{unreferenced section|date=May 2015}}

===Synthetic polyisoprene===
In 1954, Hornse was given the assignment of testing catalysts that B. F. Goodrich had licensed from Karl Ziegler.<ref name=":0" /> After verifying the claims for the polymerization of ethylene, and also for other alpha-olefins, Horne copolymerized ethylene with other olefins as a means of controlling the polyethylene density.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} With the success of the copolymerizations, he decided to try to copolymerize ethylene with isoprene with the thought of getting a copolymer that could be vulcanized with sulfur in a typical rubber recipe. While Ziegler had reported no success in polymerizing dienes, Horne attempted to copolymerize ethylene with isoprene which resulted in a mixture of cis-1,4-polyisoprene and polyethylene.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Petkewich |first1=Rachel |title=Obituaries |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/84/i19/Obituaries.html |access-date=9 June 2023 |volume=84 |issue=19 |journal=[[Chemical & Engineering News]] |date=May 8, 2006 |pages=95–96 |doi=10.1021/cen-v084n047.p095 |issn=0009-2347 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230609084435/https://cen.acs.org/articles/84/i19/Obituaries.html |archive-date=Jun 9, 2023 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

==Awards==
In 1969, he was chairman of the Gordon Conference on Hydrocarbon Chemistry. In 1974, he received the Pioneer Award from the [[American Institute of Chemists]]. In 1978, he received the Midgley Medal from the Detroit Section of the [[American Chemical Society]]. In 1980, he received the [[Charles Goodyear Medal]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Synthetic rubber pioneer Samuel Horne Jr. dies at age 82 |url=https://www.rubbernews.com/article/20060210/NEWS/302109994/synthetic-rubber-pioneer-samuel-horne-jr-dies-at-age-82 |access-date=30 January 2024 |work=Rubber and Plastics News |publisher=Crain |date=February 10, 2006}}</ref> And in 1982, he received an Honorary Doctor of Science from Emory University.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chronological Listing of Honorary Degree Recipients Emory University 1846 - present|url=http://www.emory.edu/secretary/documents/HD%20Recipients%20Master%20List%20-%201846%20to%20Present%20%2006.18.13.pdf|accessdate=24 March 2014|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140325042333/http://www.emory.edu/secretary/documents/HD%20Recipients%20Master%20List%20-%201846%20to%20Present%20%2006.18.13.pdf|archivedate=25 March 2014}}</ref>
